insights.headline: You turn crisis into arithmetic before you let yourself act, and the numbers themselves are what make the fear bearable.
insights.explanation: At 14 you built a ruled inventory of food-days before doing anything else about your father's silence. At 20, during his BP crisis, you ran a same-day scan-and-drug cost calculation instead of calling for help. At 24 you ran three-column best/medium/worst projections for both IELTS and UK migration before telling anyone. You named the function once yourself, but you did not connect it across the three moments when you told it.

writing it made something in my chest go down. Like when you finally find where the mosquito is hiding.
I did three columns. Best case, medium, worst. I even put a column for if the pound moves.

insights.would_predict: Health and Wellness: Mental and emotional health — facing a personal health scare of your own, you will research and quantify costs, timelines, statistics before you seek emotional support or say the fear out loud.

insights.headline: You tell your family about major decisions only after they're already irreversible, and you didn't see it as a rule until you said it twice.
insights.explanation: You hid the change-of-course from your father until the admission list came out. Nine years later you're hiding the IELTS exam and score from everyone but Kemi until you have "the CBT pass in my hand" or "the offer." You only recognized this as a repeated strategy mid-sentence, saying "I never thought about that" — it was operating before you could name it.

evidence.quote: I paid with my own money. I didn't tell my daddy. I told him after, when the admission list came out
That's how I did the change of course thing too, actually. Wow. I never thought about that.

insights.would_predict: Relationships: Marriage and partnership — in a future serious relationship, you will delay telling your partner about a major unilateral decision until it's already settled.

insights.headline: You believe you personally have to hold the knowledge of what's at risk in your family, and you reused the exact phrase "count what is remaining" nine years apart without noticing.
insights.explanation: Nobody assigned you the food inventory at 14 — you said so yourself. Nobody assigned you the crisis management at 20 — you pre-empted it. At 24, weighing whether to leave for the UK, you asked "who will count what is remaining," reusing the counting language from the inventory almost verbatim, nine years later, with no acknowledgment of the echo.

evidence.quote: how many days it can carry us
Who will count what is remaining.

insights.would_predict: Family and parenting: if you become a parent, you will independently track household risk without delegating or trusting a partner to hold the same information, even when told to share the load.

insights.headline: You calm yourself by making an opaque threat into a visible staged structure — steps, columns, a syllabus — and it's the visibility that works, not the outcome.
insights.explanation: The nursing handbook staircase, the NMC pathway written out step by step, and the food inventory with dates are the same move three times: an unbounded threat converted into something bounded and checkable. You named the appeal once, in the nursing account, but didn't connect it to doing the identical thing in the food-inventory and IELTS accounts.

evidence.quote: when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything
everything is steps, do step one do step two

insights.would_predict: Work and Career: Skills and competence — starting any new role, you will write your own breakdown of stages before being asked, and report calm specifically at the point the structure becomes visible.

insights.headline: You protect the people you love from the full shape of a problem while carrying the unshaped truth alone — and it's costing you more isolation over time, not less.
insights.explanation: You fictionalized a competition for your siblings, withheld the real severity of your father's BP crisis from Aunty Funmi until it was resolved, hid your migration plans from your whole family, and comforted a grieving son with a line you didn't fully believe. You alone hold the full facts each time; everyone else gets a simplified version. The shift from an elaborate invented story at 14 to a single suppressed sentence at 23 suggests the withholding is producing less relief for you as you get older, not more.

evidence.quote: I told them we were doing a competition.
I wanted to say — I didn't say anything. I said it's okay sir.

insights.would_predict: Relationships: Communication and conflict — in a future conflict with a partner or close friend, you will manage your own distress privately and offer them a simplified, reassuring account rather than what you're actually thinking.

insights.headline: You call your big decisions pure impulse, but every one of them is paired with immediate deliberate paperwork you treat as a separate, lesser thing.
insights.explanation: You said the nursing decision had "no reasoning" and that your body decides and your mouth catches up later. But the same week you went to the cyber cafe and did the change of course yourself — a deliberate administrative act. The IELTS decision is framed as something you'll "know when I know... at a bus stop," yet it's preceded and followed by extensive costed planning. You draw a line between the "real" decision and the mechanics of carrying it out, but your own account shows these as two phases of one process, not two different things.

evidence.quote: It was just the moment my body decided something and then my mouth caught up later.

insights.would_predict: Purpose: Personal mission — when you eventually choose whether to emigrate, you will describe the final choice as a sudden unplanned moment, even though deliberate preparatory steps will already be underway.

insights.headline: Across four of your five accounts, you're the one holding your family's money and crisis-knowledge without being asked — and you're now quietly weighing that role against leaving the country.
insights.explanation: The food inventory shows you as the one who calculates survival; the Aunty Funmi account shows you managing the family's relationship with its funder; the ward account shows you remembering what others forget, even for a stranger's family; the IELTS account reveals the stakes were never abstract — you weigh leaving specifically against who will be there when your father's BP crisis happens again and who will count what's remaining. None of the earlier accounts names this as a role; only the last one gestures at its weight, and even then you immediately undercut it.

insights.headline: You read unspoken family-level obligations with unusual precision and act to head them off before anyone asks you to.
insights.explanation: During your father's BP crisis, you predicted in real time that calling Aunty Funmi would create a year of implicit debt-language before it happened, and acted on that prediction under pressure. You also read, unprompted, that your father wanted medicine specifically because he'd already told his friends. This is social forecasting — modeling how information will be used before you release it — and you trust your read of other people more than you trust your own arithmetic elsewhere in your accounts.

candidates.explanation: The explicit lesson she draws ("Not how do I feel about it. The alternative — that she is simply pragmatic — doesn't explain why counting specifically calmed her chest, or why she still tracks emotionally loaded facts (dates, durations) years later while calling herself someone who doesn't keep records.

candidates.headline: She converts every crisis into a quantified system before she lets herself act, and this is what lets her act at all.
candidates.explanation: At 14 she builds a ruled inventory of food-days (E1 L26-33). At 20 she does a same-day scan/drug cost calculation instead of calling for help (E2 L41-43). At 24 she runs three-column best/medium/worst cost projections for both IELTS and UK migration (E5 L14-16, L40-41). In each case the arithmetic precedes the decision and appears to be the mechanism that makes the decision bearable, not just a record of it. Her own line names the function directly, but only for the first instance -- she doesn't connect it to the later ones herself ('I never thought about that,' E5 L32).
candidates.narrator_frame: "writing it made something in my chest go down. Like when you finally find where the mosquito is hiding" (E1 L34-35); "Not how do I feel about it. Nobody can eat how you feel about it" (E1 L64-65).
candidates.form_evidence: Numeric precision (bag-finish dates, naira totals, IELTS band scores, monthly remittance figures) appears at every point of high emotional stakes across E1, E2, E5, while feeling-language is either absent or explicitly dismissed as irrelevant.
candidates.check: E1: inventory before acting (L25-34). E2: cost calculation before acting during father's BP crisis (L41-43). E4: does last-offices procedure with 'steady hands... completely clear' mind rather than emotional processing (L46). E5: three-column financial modelling before disclosure (L13-16, L40-41). E3 is the exception -- the nursing decision itself was not calculated (L29-31) though she rationalised it with a staircase/syllabus metaphor afterward (L32-41).
candidates.counterexample: E3's core decision ('nursing... it went quiet... I didn't reason it,' L24-30) was explicitly not quantified in the moment -- it was a bodily impulse she rationalised only afterward. This shows the mechanism is not universal to decision-making, only to decisions made under threat of loss or exposure, which E3 was not (JAMB failure was already final, nothing to protect by calculating).

candidates.check: E1 L37-42, E2 L37-41, E4 L55-59, E5 L17-29. All four involve her holding complete information and dispensing a partial or false version to someone she is protecting from the full truth.

candidates.form_evidence: The specificity gradient (sensory detail highest for peripheral figures she can safely dislike or note, lowest for figures she depends on or loves) is itself the evidence; she never states a rule for who gets remembered how.

insights.headline: You turn crisis into arithmetic before you let yourself act, and the numbers themselves are what make the fear bearable.
insights.explanation: At 14 you built a ruled inventory of food-days before doing anything else about your father's silence. At 20, during his BP crisis, you ran a same-day scan-and-drug cost calculation instead of calling for help. At 24 you ran three-column best/medium/worst projections for both IELTS and UK migration before telling anyone. You named the function once yourself, but you did not connect it across the three moments when you told it.

evidence.quote: I calculated, if we eat rice three times a week, this bag will finish on such-and-such date. I even wrote the date.
writing it made something in my chest go down. Like when you finally find where the mosquito is hiding.
I did three columns. Best case, medium, worst. I even put a column for if the pound moves.

insights.counterexample: The nursing decision itself was not calculated in the moment — it came as a wordless bodily impulse under the shelter at Ojota, rationalized only afterward. So this applies to decisions made under threat of loss, not to decisions where there's nothing left to protect.
insights.confidence_note: Raised if you show the same calculate-first pattern in a fourth domain with no crisis attached; lowered if you make a comparably high-stakes decision by impulse and never go back to number it.
insights.falsifier: If you made a high-stakes decision by impulse and did not later rationalize it numerically, this pattern weakens.
insights.would_predict: Health and Wellness: Mental and emotional health — facing a personal health scare of your own, you will research and quantify costs, timelines, statistics before you seek emotional support or say the fear out loud.

insights.headline: You tell your family about major decisions only after they're already irreversible, and you didn't see it as a rule until you said it twice.

Nine years later you're hiding the IELTS exam and score from everyone but Kemi until you have "the CBT pass in my hand" or "the offer." You only recognized this as a repeated strategy mid-sentence, saying "I never thought about that" — it was operating before you could name it.

evidence.quote: I paid with my own money. I didn't tell my daddy. I told him after, when the admission list came out
That's how I did the change of course thing too, actually. Wow. I never thought about that.

insights.counterexample: With your siblings in the food-inventory year, you didn't conceal your own actions — you reframed rather than fully hid, and that audience wasn't holding authority or money over you. The pattern may be specific to disclosure toward people with power over your outcomes, not everyone you love.
insights.confidence_note: Raised if a third instance surfaces with the same delay-until-settled structure; lowered if you disclose the IELTS attempt before the CBT/offer stage as you said you would wait for.
insights.falsifier: If you disclose the IELTS attempt before the CBT/offer stage, contrary to your stated plan, this weakens as a genuine rule rather than situational caution.
insights.would_predict: Relationships: Marriage and partnership — in a future serious relationship, you will delay telling your partner about a major unilateral decision until it's already settled.

insights.headline: You believe you personally have to hold the knowledge of what's at risk in your family, and you reused the exact phrase "count what is remaining" nine years apart without noticing.
insights.explanation: Nobody assigned you the food inventory at 14 — you said so yourself. Nobody assigned you the crisis management at 20 — you pre-empted it. At 24, weighing whether to leave for the UK, you asked "who will count what is remaining," reusing the counting language from the inventory almost verbatim, nine years later, with no acknowledgment of the echo.

evidence.quote: how many days it can carry us
Who will count what is remaining.

insights.counterexample: The nursing decision itself involved no tracking or counting move beforehand — it was impulsive. This suggests the belief applies to safeguarding others, not to choices about your own life.
insights.confidence_note: Raised if this monitoring-role language shows up a third time in a new domain; lowered if you describe handing this role to a sibling or parent without anxiety.
insights.falsifier: If you expressed willingness to hand off this monitoring role to a sibling or parent without anxiety, the belief that it must be you would weaken.
insights.would_predict: Family and parenting: if you become a parent, you will independently track household risk without delegating or trusting a partner to hold the same information, even when told to share the load.

insights.headline: You calm yourself by making an opaque threat into a visible staged structure — steps, columns, a syllabus — and it's the visibility that works, not the outcome.
insights.explanation: The nursing handbook staircase, the NMC pathway written out step by step, and the food inventory with dates are the same move three times: an unbounded threat converted into something bounded and checkable. You named the appeal once, in the nursing account, but didn't connect it to doing the identical thing in the food-inventory and IELTS accounts.

evidence.quote: when you can see the whole staircase, you can climb anything
everything is steps, do step one do step two

insights.counterexample: The initial nursing decision was the opposite of this — unstructured, wordless, bodily. The system-building is a second-stage tool you reach for after the decision, not how you start one.
insights.confidence_note: Raised if a new domain shows the same calm-at-visible-structure moment; lowered if a structured plan is shown increasing your anxiety instead.
insights.falsifier: If you described a high-stakes situation where building a structured plan increased your anxiety rather than calmed you, this weakens.
insights.would_predict: Work and Career: Skills and competence — starting any new role, you will write your own breakdown of stages before being asked, and report calm specifically at the point the structure becomes visible.

insights.headline: You protect the people you love from the full shape of a problem while carrying the unshaped truth alone — and it's costing you more isolation over time, not less.
insights.explanation: You fictionalized a competition for your siblings, withheld the real severity of your father's BP crisis from Aunty Funmi until it was resolved, hid your migration plans from your whole family, and comforted a grieving son with a line you didn't fully believe. You alone hold the full facts each time; everyone else gets a simplified version. The shift from an elaborate invented story at 14 to a single suppressed sentence at 23 suggests the withholding is producing less relief for you as you get older, not more.

evidence.quote: I told them we were doing a competition.
I wanted to say — I didn't say anything. I said it's okay sir.

insights.counterexample: With your father, you did eventually tell the full truth about the change of course rather than concealing it permanently — the withholding is time-limited and strategic, not a permanent policy of deception. That softens "you deceive" to "you sequence disclosure."
insights.confidence_note: Raised if the pattern shows up a third time with increasing discomfort attached; lowered if you give someone the full unsimplified truth at comparable stakes.
insights.falsifier: If you gave the grieving son, or your siblings, the full unsimplified truth in a moment of comparable stakes, this mechanism would not hold as consistently protective withholding.
insights.would_predict: Relationships: Communication and conflict — in a future conflict with a partner or close friend, you will manage your own distress privately and offer them a simplified, reassuring account rather than what you're actually thinking.

insights.headline: You call your big decisions pure impulse, but every one of them is paired with immediate deliberate paperwork you treat as a separate, lesser thing.
insights.explanation: You said the nursing decision had "no reasoning" and that your body decides and your mouth catches up later. But the same week you went to the cyber cafe and did the change of course yourself — a deliberate administrative act. The IELTS decision is framed as something you'll "know when I know... at a bus stop," yet it's preceded and followed by extensive costed planning. You draw a line between the "real" decision and the mechanics of carrying it out, but your own account shows these as two phases of one process, not two different things.

evidence.quote: It was just the moment my body decided something and then my mouth caught up later.
I'll probably know when I know. It'll be at a bus stop or somewhere stupid like that, I'll just be standing somewhere and my mouth will say it.

insights.counterexample: The food-inventory account collapses this split — the impulse and the systematic act are the same move at the same time, with no separate later reasoning phase. The impulse-then-system split may be specific to decisions made under institutional pressure, not domestic crisis response.
insights.confidence_note: Raised if the UK decision, when it comes, follows the same pattern; lowered if a major decision happens with no administrative follow-through phase at all.
insights.falsifier: If you made a major decision with no subsequent administrative or planning phase at all, this claim that impulse and system are always paired would weaken.
insights.would_predict: Purpose: Personal mission — when you eventually choose whether to emigrate, you will describe the final choice as a sudden unplanned moment, even though deliberate preparatory steps will already be underway.

insights.headline: You read unspoken family-level obligations with unusual precision and act to head them off before anyone asks you to.
insights.explanation: During your father's BP crisis, you predicted in real time that calling Aunty Funmi would create a year of implicit debt-language before it happened, and acted on that prediction under pressure. You also read, unprompted, that your father wanted medicine specifically because he'd already told his friends. This is social forecasting — modeling how information will be used before you release it — and you trust your read of other people more than you trust your own arithmetic elsewhere in your accounts.

he had already told his friends

insights.counterexample: With the grieving son at the ward, your read was less certain — you offered a stock reassurance rather than a tailored one, suggesting this ability may be strongest inside your own family system and weaker with strangers.
insights.confidence_note: Raised if you accurately predict a third family reaction under pressure; lowered if a social prediction like this one turns out wrong.
insights.falsifier: If you had misjudged Aunty Funmi's reaction, or misjudged your father's hopes, this specific claim would weaken.
insights.would_predict: Work and Career: Leadership and collaboration — in team settings, you will be the one colleagues consult before raising a sensitive request to a manager, because you accurately predict how it will land.
